title: When Does Instant Episode Repetition Help in Reinforcement Learning? A Reproduction and Analysis of Replay Fidelity
content: Instant Episode Repetition (IER) re-executes the action sequence of the best training episode so far, open-loop, for a fixed number of later episodes. Its original evaluation reports faster learning for off-policy learners with five seeds. We reproduce its claims for soft actor-critic (SAC) on four of the original tasks with 20 seeds per arm and an analysis plan fixed before the main runs. We add the released-code schedule, a fixed repeat count, a control that copies the stored episode into the replay buffer, perturbed start states and dynamics, and CrossQ as a stronger base learner. The effect of IER depends on the task. Its difference in normalized area under the learning curve (AUC) against SAC alone is -0.090 [-0.134, -0.050] on HalfCheetah and 0.050 [0.007, 0.096] on walker-walk, a small gain that does not survive an exploratory multiple-comparison correction. Hopper and finger-turn_hard show no clear difference, and we detect no clear AUC improvement for CrossQ. After the first 200k steps, on the three tasks that still trigger replays, an open-loop replay keeps a median of under 15% of the stored return. Yet on walker-walk re-execution beats copying the episode into the buffer, and in an exploratory test it also beats replaying random past episodes, whose replays keep far more of their return. Under perturbed starts and dynamics we detect no clear reduction in the advantage of IER, and in some conditions it grows while both arms lose absolute performance. Reproducing a high return and producing useful training data are therefore different questions, and we recommend testing IER per task against the base learner. Code is available at https://github.com/alamgirakash2000/ier-stress.
